newsitem.title: USA: Clinton focuses on budget, campaign reform.
newsitem.headline: Clinton focuses on budget, campaign reform.

text.p: After celebrating his second inauguration into the wee hours, President Bill Clinton went back to business on Tuesday, opening his push for a balanced budget agreement and campaign finance reform.

Clinton, who danced at 15 inaugural balls after a day of pomp and ceremony that surrounded his swearing-in for another four years (as U.S. chief executive), symbolised the priority he places on budget-balancing with a meeting with his economic advisers as the first item on his post-inaugural schedule. The meeting was set for 1:30 p.m. EST (1830 GMT).

"I expect him to reiterate his determination to balance the budget. ... He's prepared a real, credible, common ground budget that can reach bipartisan agreement quickly if Congress is so inclined," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

Later in the day Clinton was to address the Democratic National Committee and McCurry said he would offer specific proposals to end the campaign financing practices that caused problems for the president and his party last year.

Clinton was heavily criticised for seeming to offer unusual access -- including overnight lodging in the Lincoln Bedroom of the White House -- to big contributors to his 1996 re-election campaign. Although he denied he did anything wrong, he acknowledged that campaign financing rules must be tightened to restore public confidence in the integrity of the U.S. political system.
On Feb. 6, Clinton is to send Congress his budget for the 1998 fiscal year that begins on Oct. 1 and McCurry said: "We want this budget to be treated seriously when it arrives on (Capitol) Hill.
"We believe Congress, when they look at the details of this budget, will see that we've made a good-faith effort to write a credible, sensible balanced budget for the future."

Efforts to reach a balanced-budget deal a year ago broke down amid major policy differences between the parties. The acrimonious negotiations held up passage of money bills for federal agencies and led to two partial government shutdowns.

White House officials said the Democratic president planned to go all out to compromise with the Republican-led Congress on budget legislation to take the steam out of a Republican drive to write a balanced-budget mandate into the U.S. Constitution.

Clinton gained a powerful ally in the politically charged constitutional tussle on Tuesday when Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenpan told the Senate Banking Committee he had "concerns" about a balanced budget amendment. But Greenspan conceded that "artificial" restraints on the budget -- such as those inherent in a budget amendment -- have worked surprisingly well in the past in bringing down the deficit.

The White House said Clinton was optimistic about chances for meaningful negotiations with the Republicans on a plan to balance the budget by 2002 because of private signals they have sent and their response at a luncheon after Clinton's inaugural speech to his plea for an end to partisan bickering.

Congressional Republicans "could not have been warmer and could not have been more responsive," McCurry told reporters. "The whole spirit of the day was very clearly one in which everyone laboured to be 'repairers of the breach.'"

This was a reference to Clinton's selection of a biblical passage from the prophet Isaiah to set the tone for his next four years as president. The passage exalts people who work for reconciliation and harmony.
